A source revision and a deletion change records, and a redefinition, a writer switch, and an export add no text. (b) The four HoldMem cells $(D,B)$ after a redefinition. With a key ($B{=}1$), the memory invalidates the item and re-derives it. Without a key ($B{=}0$), it keeps the old list and derives a new item only when a new record arrives. abstract: AI assistants store values that a language model derived from a person’s records under the person’s own definitions, such as their important contacts. Keeping such a value correct takes two steps: detection, noticing that an input changed, and repair, producing the correct new value. Benchmarks that score only the final answer cannot tell which step failed, and they state every change as new text. Seeing this limitation, we present MemShift, a benchmark of five shifts: source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch, and export. The first three fork a synthetic world into branches that differ only in the shift. Gold values and dependencies are fixed before any text, and a deterministic scorer replaces an LLM judge. For a memory that reports its invalidations, MemShift shows for each changed item whether the memory noticed the change and whether its repair was right. Moreover, we build a reference memory with known detection and repair to validate the measure. By evaluating four open-weight LLMs, we find that detection helps only as much as repair allows: the LLMs re-derive few values computed by the person’s definitions correctly, and programs that the LLM writes over typed records close most of the gap to exact recomputation. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zichuanxu/memshift.

sections.body: The paper studies values that an AI assistant derives from a person's records under the person's own definitions. Five shifts can make such values wrong: source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch, and export. In the example, two memories score about the same after a redefinition. One never notices the change, and 7.5% of its served values for changed definition items are right. The other re-derives them, and 6.7% are right. Existing benchmarks score only the final answer. The authors propose MemShift, which fixes gold values before any text is written, and HoldMem, a reference memory whose detection and repair are switched on and off.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Memories that store derived values can fail to notice a change or fail to repair it, and final-answer scores cannot tell which.

sections.body: Agent memories page, reflect, link, or extract facts. Benchmarks such as LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and MemoryAgentBench mostly score the final answer after new information arrives. Several recent systems pair detection with repair. MemoRepair withdraws and rebuilds derived items and assumes complete provenance. StateMem records the source records of an item and recomputes it with a language model, and its benchmark uses an LLM judge. PLANFENCE checks input versions but always replans. MemTrace varies the age of one fact, and RECON does not compare a stale store with its repaired version. MemShift adds the crossing of detection with repair, shifts that add no text, and gold values fixed before any text.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Most memory benchmarks score final answers, so a missed detection and a failed repair look the same.

sections.body: MemShift builds twelve-month worlds for one synthetic person, with six sources and 1,505–1,654 events each. A memory derives 48 items. The 42 other items are facts read from records, and six are definition items computed with the person's own rules. A deterministic evaluator fixes gold values, statuses, and dependencies before any text is written, and a deterministic scorer checks answers without an LLM judge. The shifts fork each world at the end of month nine, and the branches share every other event byte for byte. A memory that logs its invalidations gets the missed-invalidation share m, the repair correctness r, and the served accuracy a for each changed item. Update then equals (1 − m) r + m a. Other memories get only carryover.
sections.heading: The MemShift Benchmark
sections.headline: MemShift forks synthetic worlds into branches that differ only in the shift and scores each changed item on detection and repair.

sections.body: HoldMem derives each item from a 6,000-token selection of records in the item's sources. It stores a one-sentence statement with up to six cited records. Two switches set its behavior. The detection switch B is 0 when the memory only appends and never invalidates. It is 1 when each item has a key, and the key triggers invalidation and re-derivation when an input changes. The source key and the citation key are the two tested keys. The repair switch D is 0 when the writer re-derives the item. It is 1 when the memory checks the writer's value and computes the value exactly where the check fails. For 43 of 48 items, exact computation matches gold, so D=1 is an upper bound on repair. The source key invalidated 99.7%, 99.3%, and 100.0% of unchanged items after a source revision, a redefinition, and a deletion.
sections.heading: HoldMem: A Reference Memory
sections.headline: HoldMem is a reference memory whose detection and repair switches have known effects, used to validate the measure.

sections.body: Qwen3.5-9B is the default writer and reader, at temperature 0 with constrained decoding. Llama-3.1-8B, gemma-4-12B, and gpt-oss-20b each replace it as writer and reader on 10 test worlds. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 write the definition items on 10 worlds. The baselines are plain RAG with dense retrieval, an oracle context holding exactly the gold dependency records, and no-store BM25 over live records. Six existing memory systems run through their own interfaces on three-month worlds, so only storage and retrieval differ. The main study runs six HoldMem cells on 20 twelve-month test worlds after a source revision, a redefinition, and a deletion. Each estimate has a 95% world-bootstrap interval from 2,000 draws.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Experiments test four open-weight models, two Claude writers, and six existing memory systems on fixed test worlds.

sections.body: The main study uses twelve-month worlds with Qwen3.5-9B as writer and reader. After a redefinition, a key raised Update by +0.2 pp with the writer's re-derivation, by +25.4 pp with the writer's programs, and by +26.9 pp with exact recomputation. The same interaction holds for all four open-weight models. On changed definition items, each open-weight writer re-derived at most 25% correctly after every shift, while exact recomputation got at least 91% right. Programs over typed records keep most of the interaction. A citation key notices every redefinition but missed 16.9% of changed items after a source revision, mostly records that joined later. A Claude writer that sees every record re-derived 91.8% of changed definition items correctly. The source-key contrasts replicate on 20 fresh worlds.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: A detection key helps only when repair is good, and open-weight writers re-derive at most 25% of changed definition values correctly.

sections.body: A key's value depends on the repair that follows it. A language model's re-derivation is not exact, and it is weakest for values that aggregate many records under a person's definition. A key helps there mainly with exact recomputation or with programs over typed records. A strong writer that sees every record comes close, but it must read every record at each re-derivation. A diagnosis names the failing term and item class, and the class shows which fix helps. On three-month worlds, the ranking of the six HoldMem cells by Update after a source revision nearly matches their ranking after a redefinition, with Spearman 0.94 [0.75, 1.00]. The ranking of the six native systems does not, with 0.52 [-0.09, 0.94]. The authors recommend reporting m and r by item class.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Repair decides what detection is worth, and a final-answer score hides which step failed.

sections.body: MemShift is a benchmark for the derived personal memory of language models. It scores each item that a shift changes on detection and repair, against gold fixed before any text. Detection helps only as much as repair allows. Repair fails on items that the person's definitions compute, and programs over typed records close most of that gap. Keys built from the writer's citations miss records that join an item later. A memory's accuracy after a change reflects its detection and its repair together. Future work could test memories in which a language model decides invalidation, and real records with vaguer definitions.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: MemShift scores detection and repair separately, and typed-record programs close most of the repair gap on definition items.

sections.body: The worlds are synthetic and rendered from templates. Each definition is a one-sentence rule over structured fields, so real records and vaguer definitions may behave differently. Only a small share of message text was rewritten by a model, and field extraction was tested only on model-written prose. The reference memory is designed by the authors, and D=1 runs the gold evaluator, so it is an upper bound and not a system under test. Native systems ran on three-month worlds at D=0 through adapters, with noisy ingestion, and the tested Mem0 release only adds memories. The main writers are open-weight models with 8–27B parameters. Update depends on the reader and on the serving format, so the signs of effects generalize better than their levels. Holm and Benjamini–Hochberg corrections keep 35 and 36 of the 36 intervals that exclude zero.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Findings rest on synthetic worlds with codified definitions and 20 test worlds, so absolute levels may not transfer.

sections.body: The work concerns systems that store what AI assistants know about individual people. Measuring whether that knowledge stays correct can make assistants more reliable and make personal data easier to move. Persistent, portable personal profiles, however, raise privacy risks. All MemShift worlds are synthetic, no personal data was collected, and no human subjects were involved. Derived profiles still hold facts about third parties, and exported provenance reveals which sources and models produced each item. The benchmark scores consent revocation, and every stored derived memory the authors measured still leaks after a revocation. Writer programs run only on synthetic records, in a separate process with a time limit and a memory cap. A restricted interpreter accepts only listed syntax and built-in functions.
sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.headline: Benchmark uses only synthetic data, but the work concerns personal profiles that could raise privacy risks.

sections.body: Worlds, shifts, and probes are generated deterministically from seeds. A deterministic scorer checks every answer without an LLM judge. Open-weight models run at temperature 0 with constrained decoding, except for sampled program sets at temperature 0.7. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 ran through Anthropic's API with the settings listed in Section C.7. Each run records its code version, world seeds, model revisions, and output hashes in a manifest. The repository holds the code, the generator, the worlds, the gold labels, all model responses, and the run manifests. It regenerates every number in the paper.
sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.headline: Worlds, shifts, and probes are generated from seeds with no LLM judge, and the repository regenerates every number in the paper.

sections.body: The appendix extends the related work with memory systems, stale-value studies, knowledge editing, and dependency tracking. It groups provenance, portability, consent, and agent benchmarks by the question each answers for MemShift. Table 6 compares MemShift with 15 benchmarks on properties read from their papers. Further sections give failure-mode probes, including a writer program for working hours that never ran, and the views of native systems. The datasheet covers seeds for each split, collection and labeling, intended uses, the MIT code license, and the CC BY 4.0 data license.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers extended related work, stale-value studies, a benchmark audit, mechanics of dependency tracking, and a datasheet.
